beforeRecord.q: Which per-unit correction fits the garments graph, and how does it change private incentives?
options: A $6 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $4 tax; it makes the decision-maker account for the marginal external effect.
A $6 tax collected as a fixed fee from each firm; it creates the same marginal incentive as charging $6 on each garment.
A $15 per-garment tax; producers should pay the full social marginal cost in addition to their private marginal cost.
beforeRecord.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.

beforeRecord.q: Treat quantity as continuous. A council budgets $700 million to expand from 10 to 30 miles, with no fixed or financing costs. Which expansion cost, net benefit and budget assessment follow from the graph?
options: Cost $600 million and net benefit $200 million; the budget is sufficient and the expansion raises welfare.
Cost $500 million and net benefit $300 million; the budget is sufficient and the expansion raises welfare.
Cost $500 million and net benefit $300 million; affordability alone proves that any further expansion raises welfare.

beforeRecord.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.

afterRecord.commonError: Assuming the static model settles every long-run policy question.

before.imageAlt: Economics diagram: COST-03. Details are provided in the graph description.

The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 4) and (40, 6). The dashed red line labeled S1 slopes upward through (0, 2) and (80, 6). The solid blue line labeled D0 slopes downward through (0, 8) and (160, 0). The dashed blue line labeled D1 slopes downward through (0, 10) and (200, 0). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (40, 6). Point B marks the S1–D1 intersection at (80, 6). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

after.imageAlt: Concave production-function graph with labeled points A and B.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is Capital per worker from 0 to 100 and the vertical axis is Output per worker from 0 to 60. A smooth upward-sloping blue curve becomes flatter as capital per worker increases. Point A is at capital per worker 20 and output per worker 28.53. Point B is at capital per worker 40 and output per worker 36.37. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides connect each point to its axis values.

after.imageAlt: U.S. dollar market with downward-sloping demand D0 and upward-sloping supply S0 intersecting at A.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar. The horizontal axis is the quantity of U.S. dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 and upward-sloping S0 intersect at A, quantity 100 and exchange rate 1.0.

after.imageAlt: Dollar demand shifts right from D0 to D1 while upward-sloping supply S0 remains fixed.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand shifts right from solid D0 to dashed D1 along unchanged upward-sloping S0. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 1.2.

after.imageAlt: Upward-sloping dollar supply shifts right from S0 to S1 along demand D0.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand D0 is unchanged while supply shifts right from solid S0 to dashed S1. Equilibrium moves from A at quantity 100 and rate 1.0 to B at quantity 150 and rate 0.8.

after.imageAlt: Dollar demand and upward-sloping supply both shift right, from D0 and S0 to D1 and S1.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand and supply both shift right. Original equilibrium A is quantity 100 and rate 1.0; final equilibrium B is quantity 200 and rate 1.0. Solid curves are D0 and S0; dashed curves are D1 and S1. D1 crosses S0 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 1.2; D0 crosses S1 at approximately quantity 150 and rate 0.8. These two crossings have no point labels or dashed coordinate guides.

after.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market with downward-sloping demand D0 and upward-sloping supply S0.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar. The horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 intersects upward-sloping S0. No numerical ticks or point labels are shown.

after.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing demand shifting right from D0 to D1 with supply S0 unchanged.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Dashed demand D1 lies right of solid D0 while upward-sloping S0 is unchanged. The new intersection is above and right of the original intersection. No numerical ticks are shown.

after.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing upward-sloping supply shifting right from S0 to S1 with demand D0 unchanged.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Dashed supply S1 lies right of solid S0 while demand D0 is unchanged. The new intersection is below and right of the original intersection. No numerical ticks are shown.

after.imageAlt: Conceptual dollar market showing demand and upward-sloping supply both shifting right.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Demand shifts right from D0 to D1 and supply shifts right from S0 to S1. The displayed shifts raise equilibrium quantity while leaving the exchange rate at the same vertical position. No numerical ticks are shown.

after.imageAlt: Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1 along D0 equals NX0.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 at quantity 100 to S1 equals NCO1 at quantity 50. Equilibrium moves from A at rate 1.0 to B at rate 1.5.

after.imageAlt: Conceptual Mankiw-model dollar market with vertical supply shifting left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1.
after.graphDescription: The vertical axis is foreign currency per U.S. dollar and the horizontal axis is the quantity of dollars exchanged. Downward-sloping D0 equals NX0. Vertical supply shifts left from S0 equals NCO0 to S1 equals NCO1, so the new intersection is above and left of the original intersection. No numerical ticks or point labels are shown.
